// question: 1
::P5Q1 Two parts out of three::[html]<p>You run this and nothing is drawn\:</p><pre><code>ggplot(students, aes(x \= attendance_pct))</code></pre><p>What do you actually see, and why?</p>{
=[html]<p>An empty panel with a correctly scaled x axis, the geom has not been named yet</p>#[html]<p>Correct. Look at the axis\: ggplot2 has already read the column and chosen the breaks. It is waiting to be told what shape to draw.</p>
~[html]<p>An error, because the plot is incomplete</p>#[html]<p>No, and that is what makes it confusing. ggplot2 draws what it can and says nothing about what is missing, so there is no message to read, just an empty panel.</p>
~[html]<p>A histogram, <code>geom_histogram()</code> is the default for one numeric column</p>#[html]<p>There is no default geom. ggplot2 never guesses what shape you meant; every plot names its geom explicitly, which is what makes the code readable.</p>
~[html]<p>Nothing at all, a blank white screen with no axes</p>#[html]<p>Not quite. You get the grey panel and a scaled axis, which is a useful signal\: it tells you the data and the mapping arrived safely and only the geom is missing.</p>
####[html]<p>You have named the data and the aesthetics but not the geom, so ggplot2 has drawn everything it can\: the panel and a correctly scaled x axis, and nothing on top of it. Miss a part and you get a blank picture rather than an error, which is confusing the first time, add <code>+ geom_histogram(binwidth \= 5)</code> and the bars appear.</p>
}

// question: 2
::P5Q2 What joins the layers::[html]<p>Everywhere else in this workshop you join steps with the native pipe. What joins one ggplot2 <em>layer</em> to the next?</p>{
=[html]<p><code>+</code></p>#[html]<p>Correct, the one exception to the pipe you will meet in these two days.</p>
~[html]<p><code>|&gt;</code>, the same as everywhere else</p>#[html]<p>Everybody does this once. <code>ggplot(...) |&gt; geom_histogram()</code> complains about a missing argument, because the pipe puts the plot where the geom expected something else. Layers take <code>+</code>.</p>
~[html]<p><code>%&gt;%</code></p>#[html]<p>No, that is the older pipe, and it fails here for the same reason <code>|&gt;</code> does. Neither pipe adds a layer; only <code>+</code> does.</p>
~[html]<p><code>&amp;</code></p>#[html]<p>No. <code>&amp;</code> is logical "and", used inside conditions. It does have a role in combining <em>whole plots</em> in the patchwork package, which is a different job from adding a layer to one plot.</p>
####[html]<p><code>+</code>, and it is history rather than logic\: ggplot2 was written in 2007, years before R had a pipe, and already had its own way of stacking layers. The rule that keeps you out of trouble, <code>|&gt;</code> moves a table from one verb to the next; <code>+</code> adds a layer or setting to a plot you have already started. You will often use both in one expression\: pipe the data into <code>ggplot()</code>, then add layers with <code>+</code>.</p>
}

// question: 3
::P5Q3 Bin width is not a detail::[html]<p>You draw the same histogram three times, with <code>binwidth \= 2</code>, then <code>5</code>, then <code>10</code>. Which statement is true?</p>{
=[html]<p>The three plots can suggest genuinely different things about the data, so it is worth looking at more than one</p>#[html]<p>Correct, and this is a habit, not a one-off. Try two or three bin widths before you describe a distribution in writing.</p>
~[html]<p>The choice is cosmetic; the distribution is the distribution</p>#[html]<p>The distribution is, but the picture you draw of it is not. A wide bin can merge two separate peaks into one, and a narrow one can turn ordinary noise into apparent structure, both change the conclusion a reader draws.</p>
~[html]<p><code>binwidth</code> sets the number of bars, so 10 gives ten bars</p>#[html]<p>That is <code>bins</code>, a different argument. <code>binwidth</code> is the width of each bin in the units of the data, so <code>binwidth \= 10</code> on a percentage means bars covering 0–10%, 10–20%, and so on.</p>
~[html]<p>You should always use the default, because ggplot2 chooses correctly</p>#[html]<p>ggplot2 explicitly does not claim to\: leave it out and it uses 30 bins with a message telling you to pick a better value. That message is advice worth taking.</p>
####[html]<p><code>binwidth</code> decides how much of the shape of the data survives. At 2 the histogram is spiky and you can see individual clumps of students; at 10 it is smooth and you may have flattened away something real. There is no correct answer, which is exactly why you should look at more than one before deciding what your data says.</p>
}

// question: 4
::P5Q4 Warning or error::[html]<p>Your boxplot appears, and underneath it R prints\:</p><pre><code>Removed 7 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range</code></pre><p>What has happened?</p>{
=[html]<p>A warning\: seven students have a missing value in that column, so they could not be drawn, the plot is fine</p>#[html]<p>Correct, and worth checking rather than ignoring\: seven is the number you should have expected.</p>
~[html]<p>An error\: the plot is invalid and must not be used</p>#[html]<p>No, you have a plot, which is how you know this was a warning rather than an error. Errors produce no result at all. Beginners often stop at the first red text; read it instead.</p>
~[html]<p>Seven outliers were automatically excluded from the plot</p>#[html]<p>No, and it matters that these are different things. ggplot2 never removes outliers on your behalf, outliers are drawn as the dots beyond the whiskers. These seven rows have no value at all.</p>
~[html]<p>The dataset is corrupt and should be downloaded again</p>#[html]<p>The missing values in this dataset are deliberate, because real data has them. Learning to read a message that tells you how many were dropped is more useful than working with data in which nothing is ever missing.</p>
####[html]<p>A <strong>warning</strong> means <em>I did it, and here is something you should know</em>. An <strong>error</strong> means <em>I could not do it, there is no result</em>. Seven students in this cohort have no <code>burnout_score</code>, and you cannot draw a box around a value that does not exist, so ggplot2 dropped them and said so. Read the number and check it is the number of missing values you expected\: if you thought two were missing and R says seven, you have learned something about your data.</p>
}
